What is .NET?: .NET is a free, cross-platform, open-source developer platform. It includes .NET Core (modern), .NET Framework (Windows-only legacy), and .NET 5+ (unified). Choose the right runtime for your scenario.
Project Types & Templates: .NET provides project templates via `dotnet new`: console, classlib, web (ASP.NET Core), mvc, webapi, blazor, xunit, maui, worker, and more. Each generates the right .csproj structure.

dotnet new list                      # List all templates
dotnet new console -n MyConsole       # Console app
dotnet new webapi -n MyApi            # Web API
dotnet new classlib -n MyLib          # Class library
dotnet new xunit -n MyTests           # Test project
IDE & Editor Choices: C# development works in Visual Studio (full IDE), Visual Studio Code (lightweight with C# Dev Kit), JetBrains Rider (cross-platform), or the CLI with any editor. The .NET CLI is universal.

# VS Code with C# Dev Kit
dotnet build          # Build all projects
dotnet test           # Run all tests
dotnet publish -c Release  # Publish for production
dotnet format         # Auto-format code
Top-Level Statements: C# 9+ top-level statements eliminate boilerplate Program class and Main method. The compiler generates them automatically, enabling script-like entry points.
File-Scoped Namespaces: C# 10 file-scoped namespaces remove one level of indentation. Use `namespace X;` syntax at the top of the file instead of a block. All declarations in the file belong to that namespace.
Project Structure & SDKs: .NET projects use SDK-style `.csproj` files. SDKs: `Microsoft.NET.Sdk` (console, lib), `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` (ASP.NET), `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Worker` (background services), `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Maui` (cross-platform). Project structure: `Program.cs` entry point, `.cs` classes, `Properties/launchSettings.json`, `appsettings.json` for config. Use `TargetFramework` (`net8.0`, `netstandard2.0`). Multiple targets with `<TargetFrameworks>`.

<!-- SDK-style .csproj (console/library) -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.0.3" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

// Program.cs — top-level statements
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapGet("/", () => "Hello World!");
app.Run();

// Class library project targets multiple frameworks
// <TargetFrameworks>net8.0;netstandard2.0;net48</TargetFrameworks>

// Directory structure:
// MyApp/
// ├── MyApp.csproj
// ├── Program.cs
// ├── Services/
// │   └── MyService.cs
// ├── Models/
// │   └── Person.cs
// ├── Properties/
// │   └── launchSettings.json
// └── appsettings.json

Primitive Types: C# has built-in value types: integral (byte, short, int, long), floating-point (float, double, decimal), character (char), boolean (bool). Each maps to a .NET struct in System namespace.
var & Implicit Typing: The `var` keyword tells the compiler to infer the type from the right-hand expression. It is strongly typed at compile time. Use it when the type is obvious from context, but prefer explicit types for public APIs.
object & dynamic: `object` is the universal base type (requires casting). `dynamic` bypasses compile-time type checking and resolves at runtime. Use `dynamic` sparingly — it sacrifices safety for flexibility (COM, JSON, DLR scenarios).
Nullable Value Types: Value types (structs) can be made nullable with the `?` suffix (e.g., int?, bool?). Nullable<T> wraps the value with HasValue/Value properties. Use null-conditional operators to handle null safely.
Nullable Reference Types: C# 8+ nullable reference types enable compile-time null-state analysis. Types are non-nullable by default; use `?` suffix to allow null. Enable via `#nullable enable` or in .csproj. The compiler emits warnings for unsafe dereferences.
Null-Forgiving Operator: The `!` postfix operator (null-forgiving / dammit operator) suppresses nullable warnings when you know a value isn't null despite the compiler's analysis. Use cautiously.
Constants & Readonly: `const` is a compile-time constant (implicitly static, no modifiers). `readonly` is a runtime constant set in the constructor. `static readonly` is like a constant that can be computed at runtime.
Tuple Types: C# 7+ tuples provide lightweight multi-value grouping with named fields. ValueTuple structs avoid heap allocation. Tuples are great for internal use; prefer records for public APIs.

Arithmetic & Assignment: Standard arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) work on numeric types. Assignment can be combined (+=, -=, etc.). The increment (++) and decrement (--) operators have prefix/postfix forms with different evaluation order.

int a = 10, b = 3;
Console.WriteLine(a + b);  // 13
Console.WriteLine(a - b);  // 7
Console.WriteLine(a * b);  // 30
Console.WriteLine(a / b);  // 3 (integer division)
Console.WriteLine(a % b);  // 1

int x = 5;
Console.WriteLine(x++);     // 5 (post-increment)
Console.WriteLine(++x);     // 7 (pre-increment)
x += 10; Console.WriteLine(x); // 17
Comparison & Equality: Comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) work on value types. For reference types, == compares references by default; override Equals and == for value semantics. Records have built-in value equality.
Logical & Bitwise: Logical operators (&&, ||, !) short-circuit. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) operate on integer bits. Use `&&` instead of `&` and `||` instead of `|` for boolean logic to benefit from short-circuit evaluation.

bool a = true, b = false;
Console.WriteLine(a && b);  // False (short-circuits)
Console.WriteLine(a || b);  // True (short-circuits)
Console.WriteLine(!a);      // False

int x = 0b1100, y = 0b1010;
Console.WriteLine(x & y);   // 1000 (8)
Console.WriteLine(x | y);   // 1110 (14)
Console.WriteLine(x ^ y);   // 0110 (6)
Console.WriteLine(~x);      // ...0011
Console.WriteLine(x << 2);  // 110000 (48)
Null-Conditional Operator: The `?.` operator safely accesses members of a possibly-null expression. It short-circuits to null if the left operand is null. Chain multiple `?.` or combine with `??` for fallback values.
Null-Coalescing Operators: `??` returns the left operand if it's not null, otherwise the right operand. `??=` (C# 8+) assigns the right operand to the left only if the left is null. Both short-circuit.
Switch Expressions: C# 8+ switch expressions provide concise, expression-based pattern matching. Unlike switch statements, they produce a value. Supports type patterns, when guards, property patterns, discards, and relational patterns.
Conditional Operator: The ternary `?:` operator evaluates a boolean condition and returns one of two expressions. Use for inline conditional values; avoid nesting for readability.

if / else if / else: Standard conditional branching. Use `if` for boolean conditions, chain with `else if` for multiple paths, and `else` as the fallback. Can use pattern matching in conditions with `is` expressions.
Switch Statement: Switch statements evaluate an expression against multiple case patterns. C# 7+ added type patterns, when guards, and the `_` discard. Cases can fall through with `goto case`, but typically each case has a `break`.
Pattern Matching: C# pattern matching includes type patterns, property patterns, positional patterns (with deconstruction), var patterns, discard patterns, relational patterns (`<`, `>`, `>=`), and logical patterns (`and`, `or`, `not`).
for Loop: The classic `for` loop uses an initializer, condition, and iterator. Perfect for indexed iteration, reverse loops, and scenarios where the iteration count is known. Declare the counter variable inline for scoped access.
foreach Loop: `foreach` iterates over any type implementing IEnumerable or IEnumerable<T>. The iterator variable is read-only inside the loop. For arrays, the compiler optimizes with a `for` loop internally.
while & do-while: `while` checks the condition before each iteration (zero or more runs). `do-while` checks after (always runs at least once). Use when the iteration count isn't known upfront.
break, continue, goto: `break` exits the current loop. `continue` skips to the next iteration. `goto` jumps to a labeled statement (use rarely). `return` exits the method entirely. Use `break` in loops and switch cases.
using Declaration: C# 8+ using declarations automatically dispose resources when the variable goes out of scope. Eliminates the nesting of traditional `using` statements. Works with IDisposable and IAsyncDisposable.

Method Basics: Methods encapsulate reusable logic. They have a signature (name, return type, parameters), a body, and an access modifier. C# supports method overloading (same name, different parameters). Methods can be static or instance.
Parameter Modifiers (ref, in, out): `ref` passes a reference to the variable (read-write). `in` passes by reference but is read-only (avoids copying for large structs). `out` passes by reference for returning values; the method must assign it before returning.
params Keyword: The `params` keyword allows a variable number of arguments. The parameter must be a single-dimensional array and must be the last parameter. The compiler generates the array automatically.
Optional & Named Parameters: Optional parameters have default values and can be omitted. Named arguments let you specify parameters by name, enabling skipping optional ones and improving readability for boolean/optional parameters.
Expression-Bodied Members: C# 6+ expression-bodied members use `=>` for concise single-expression methods, properties, and operators. Available for methods, get-only properties, constructors, finalizers, and operators.
Local Functions: C# 7+ local functions are nested methods inside another method. They capture variables from the enclosing scope, support generics, async, and even attributes. Great for helper logic that shouldn't leak.
Return Values & Multiple Returns: Methods return a single value. Return multiple values using tuples, out parameters, or a custom class/record. Tuples are lightweight; records are better for public APIs. Use `ValueTuple` for zero-allocation returns.
Delegates & Lambda Expressions: Delegates are type-safe function pointers: `Func<T,R>` (return), `Action<T>` (void), `Predicate<T>` (bool return). Custom: `delegate int Transformer(int x)`. Lambda syntax: `(param) => expr`, `(param) => { stmts }`. Closure captures outer variables. `async` lambdas: `Func<Task> f = async () => await Work()`. Multicast delegates chain multiple handlers. Event pattern built on delegates.

Classes & Objects: Classes are reference types that serve as blueprints for objects. They encapsulate data (fields, properties) and behavior (methods). Use `new` to create instances. Classes support inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.
Fields & Properties: Fields store internal state. Properties expose fields with get/set accessors, enabling validation, computed values, and lazy initialization. Auto-properties generate backing fields automatically (C# 3+).
Init Setters & Required Members: C# 9 `init` setters enable object initializer-only property assignment (immutable after construction). C# 11 `required` members force callers to provide a value during initialization. Both support object/collection initializer patterns.
Primary Constructors: C# 12 primary constructors allow parameter declaration directly on the class/struct/record. Parameters are in scope throughout the class body. For classes, they don't auto-generate properties (unlike records). Capture them explicitly if needed.
Record Types: C# 9 records provide value semantics by default: positional construction, immutable properties (with init), value-based equality, `with` expressions for non-destructive mutation, and concise deconstruction. Use `record class` (reference) or `record struct` (value).
Inheritance: C# supports single class inheritance. Use `:` to derive, `virtual` for overridable methods, `override` for specialization, `abstract` for forced implementation, `sealed` to prevent further inheritance. Base class constructors chain via `: base()`.
Polymorphism: Polymorphism allows derived types to be treated as base types. Virtual method dispatch calls the most derived override at runtime. Interface polymorphism enables unrelated types to share contracts. Use `is` and `as` for type-safe casting.
Abstract Classes & Sealed: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated, serving as base types with partial implementation. `abstract` members have no body and must be overridden. `sealed` on a class prevents inheritance entirely; on a method it stops further overriding.
Static Members & Classes: Static classes contain only static members and cannot be instantiated. Static members belong to the type, not instances. Static constructors run once per type before any static member access. Extension methods must be in static classes.
Object Initializers: Object initializers set properties/fields at creation without requiring a constructor. Collection initializers add items inline. Works with `init` setters and `required` members (C# 11+).

Interface Basics: Interfaces define contracts with methods, properties, events, and indexers. A class/struct can implement multiple interfaces. Interfaces enable loose coupling, polymorphism, and dependency injection. C# 8+ allows default implementations.
Default Interface Methods: C# 8+ default interface methods allow adding members to interfaces without breaking existing implementations. Implementations can override the default. Useful for API evolution and trait-like patterns. Not available in .NET Framework 4.8.
Generic Constraints: Constraints restrict type parameters: `where T : class` (reference), `struct` (value), `notnull` (non-nullable), `new()` (parameterless constructor), base class, interface, or `unmanaged` (blittable). Multiple constraints are stacked.
Covariance & Contravariance: Covariance (`out`) allows using a more derived type in output positions (e.g., `IEnumerable<Dog>` as `IEnumerable<Animal>`). Contravariance (`in`) allows less derived input (e.g., `IComparer<Animal>` as `IComparer<Dog>`). Only applies to interfaces/delegates with reference types.
Generic Methods: Type parameters can be defined on methods (not just classes). The compiler infers types from arguments. Generic methods enable type-safe algorithms without boxing. Combine with constraints for additional capabilities.
IDisposable & IAsyncDisposable: IDisposable defines a deterministic cleanup pattern. The `using` statement ensures Dispose() is called even on exceptions. `IAsyncDisposable` (C# 8+) enables async cleanup with `await using`. Implement the dispose pattern properly for classes holding unmanaged resources.
Variance: in/out: C# generics support covariance (`out`) and contravariance (`in`) for interfaces and delegates. `out T`: can use as return type (produce). `in T`: can use as parameter type (consume). Covariant: `IEnumerable<out T>` — `IEnumerable<string>` is `IEnumerable<object>`. Contravariant: `Action<in T>` — `Action<object>` is `Action<string>`. Only safe in one direction.

Arrays: Fixed-size, zero-indexed collections of elements of the same type. Arrays are reference types with a fixed length set at creation. Supports multi-dimensional (rectangular) and jagged (array-of-arrays) forms.
List<T>: List<T> is a generic dynamic array that grows as needed. Provides O(1) index access, O(n) insert/remove at arbitrary positions. Use for ordered collections where size changes. Implements IList<T>, ICollection<T>, IEnumerable<T>.
Dictionary<TKey, TValue>: Dictionary provides O(1) key-value lookups via hash table. Keys must be unique and properly implement GetHashCode/Equals. Use TryGetValue for safe access. Use ConcurrentDictionary for thread-safe scenarios.
HashSet<T> & SortedSet<T>: HashSet<T> is an unordered set with O(1) add/remove/lookup. SortedSet<T> maintains sorted order (O(log n)). Both implement ISet<T> with set operations: UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith, SymmetricExceptWith.
Queue<T> & Stack<T>: Queue<T> is FIFO (Enqueue/Dequeue/Peek). Stack<T> is LIFO (Push/Pop/Peek). Both use arrays internally with O(1) amortized operations. Use for breadth-first vs depth-first processing patterns.
LINQ Basics: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) enables querying any IEnumerable<T> with SQL-like syntax. Query syntax (`from x in xs where ...`) or method syntax (`.Where().Select()`) produce the same IL. Deferred execution until enumeration.
LINQ Methods Deep: LINQ provides projection (Select, SelectMany), filtering (Where, OfType), ordering (OrderBy, ThenBy, Reverse), grouping (GroupBy, ToLookup), joins (Join, GroupJoin), aggregation (Sum, Average, Min, Max, Count, Aggregate), set ops (Distinct, Union, Intersect, Except), partitioning (Skip, Take, SkipWhile, TakeWhile), and element ops (First, Last, Single, ElementAt, DefaultIfEmpty).
LINQ GroupBy & Joins: GroupBy partitions sequences into groups with a key. Join performs inner joins on matching keys. GroupJoin creates a hierarchical result (left outer join). Zip combines two sequences element-by-element. All support custom equality comparers.
Concurrent Collections: System.Collections.Concurrent provides thread-safe collections: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,T> (lock-free ops), ConcurrentQueue<T> (FIFO), ConcurrentStack<T> (LIFO), ConcurrentBag<T> (unordered), BlockingCollection<T> (bounded producer/consumer).
PLINQ (Parallel LINQ): PLINQ automatically parallelizes LINQ queries via `AsParallel()`. Uses partitioning and thread pooling. Control parallelism with `WithDegreeOfParallelism`, `WithExecutionMode`, `WithCancellation`. Results can be unordered (`AsUnordered`) for better performance.

try / catch / finally: Structured exception handling: `try` guards code, `catch` handles exceptions (specific or general), `finally` always executes (cleanup). Exceptions bubble up the call stack until caught. Unhandled exceptions crash the process.
Exception Filters (when): C# `catch` with `when` filters exceptions without unwinding the stack first. Log or conditionally catch: `catch (Exception ex) when (Log(ex))`. Filter runs before the catch block; false skips to next handler. Useful for distinguishing error types by runtime data. Can catch by type and filter on `ex.Data`, `ex.HResult`, or custom properties. Stack trace preserved since stack isn't unwound if filter returns false.
Custom Exceptions: Create custom exceptions by inheriting from Exception. Follow best practices: end class name with `Exception`, implement the three standard constructors, use serialization if needed, provide additional properties for rich error data.
Guard Clauses & Argument Validation: Validate arguments early using guard clauses. Use `ArgumentException`, `ArgumentNullException`, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. C# 11 lets you specify the nameof parameter. Consider using `ThrowHelper` patterns or a library like Ardalis.GuardClauses to reduce inlining.
Throw Helpers: Throw helpers are `static` local/member methods that throw exceptions. The JIT sees `throw` as a cold path and doesn't inline the helper, reducing method size and improving performance. Use for validation-heavy APIs.
Result Pattern (Functional Error Handlin: Instead of exceptions for expected failures, use a Result type to return success/failure explicitly. Common in domain-driven design. Integrates with `switch` expressions for exhaustive handling. Libraries like FluentResults or OneOf formalize this pattern.

async / await Basics: async/await enables non-blocking asynchronous code. async methods return Task, Task<T>, or ValueTask<T>. Await suspends the method without blocking the thread. Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code to avoid capturing SynchronizationContext.
Task & Task<T>: Task represents an async operation. Task<T> produces a value. Tasks can be awaited, combined (WhenAll, WhenAny), or continued (ContinueWith, but prefer await). Status tracks lifecycle: Created, WaitingForActivation, RanToCompletion, Faulted, Canceled.
Cancellation: CancellationToken from CancellationTokenSource enables cooperative cancellation. Pass to async methods. Throw OperationCanceledException when cancelled. Use Register for callbacks. Linked tokens combine multiple sources.
ValueTask & ValueTask<T>: ValueTask<T> (C# 7+) is a struct that can wrap a synchronous result or a Task<T>. Avoids allocation when the result is already available. Use only for hot paths where sync completion is common. Can only be awaited once (use AsTask() for multiple).
Async Streams (IAsyncEnumerable): C# 8+ async streams enable async iteration with `await foreach`. Methods return `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` using `yield return` with `await`. Supports CancellationToken, ConfigureAwait, and LINQ via System.Linq.Async.
Channel<T>: System.Threading.Channels provides thread-safe producer/consumer queues. Bounded channels (backpressure) limit capacity; unbounded grow indefinitely. ChannelReader exposes ReadAllAsync() for async streams. Perfect for pub/sub and pipeline patterns.
Task Parallel Library (Dataflow): System.Threading.Tasks.Dataflow provides actor-like message passing blocks: BufferBlock<T>, ActionBlock<T>, TransformBlock<TInput,TOutput>, BatchBlock<T>, JoinBlock<T1,T2>. Link blocks into pipelines with completion propagation. Fine-grained parallelism control.
Thread Synchronization: Use `lock` for mutual exclusion (Monitor syntactic sugar). For finer control: Monitor (Wait/Pulse), Mutex (cross-process), Semaphore/SemaphoreSlim (counting), ReaderWriterLockSlim (read-heavy), Barrier (phased), CountdownEvent, ManualResetEvent. Prefer higher-level primitives.
Parallel.For / Parallel.ForEach: System.Threading.Tasks.Parallel provides parallel loops: Parallel.For (indexed), Parallel.ForEach (enumerable), Parallel.Invoke (multiple actions). Controls degree of parallelism and supports thread-local state (overloads). Use for CPU-bound parallel work.

File & Directory Operations: System.IO provides File (static methods), FileInfo (instance), Directory, DirectoryInfo, and Path. Read/write text, bytes, or lines. Use async methods for I/O-bound work. Guard against path traversal and IO exceptions.
StreamReader / StreamWriter: StreamReader/StreamWriter provide text-level access over streams. Support different encodings, buffer sizes, and async operations. Use `using` for proper disposal. FileStream provides raw byte-level access.
System.Text.Json: System.Text.Json (high-performance, UTF-8) serializes/deserializes JSON. Supports source generators (AOT-friendly), custom converters, ignore/modify serialization via attributes, JsonDocument (DOM), and JsonSerializerOptions for configuration.
System.Text.Json Source Generators: C# 9+ source generators for System.Text.Json eliminate runtime reflection. Declare partial classes with [JsonSerializerSerializable] (or [JsonSourceGenerationOptions]) for compile-time serialization. Enables native AOT, reduces startup, avoids reflection.
XML Serialization: XmlSerializer serializes to/from XML. Control output with attributes ([XmlElement], [XmlAttribute], [XmlIgnore], [XmlArray]). Supports complex object graphs. XDocument/Linq to Xml provides LINQ-friendly XML manipulation.
Binary Serialization (obsolete): BinaryFormatter (now obsolete/unsafe) serializes object graphs including private members. .NET 8+ throws PlatformNotSupportedException. Use JSON, Protobuf, or MessagePack instead. Never use BinaryFormatter in new code due to security risks (deserialization vulnerabilities).
Protocol Buffers (Protobuf): Google.Protobuf provides compact, cross-language serialization via .proto definitions. Much smaller/faster than JSON. Use with gRPC. Generate C# classes from .proto files. Ideal for high-performance internal services and wire protocols.

Span<T> & ReadOnlySpan<T>: Span<T> is a stack-allocated ref struct providing safe, allocation-free views over contiguous memory (arrays, strings, native memory). No heap allocation. Ideal for high-performance string parsing, buffer manipulation, and slicing operations.
Memory<T> & ReadOnlyMemory<T>: Memory<T> is the heap-friendly counterpart to Span<T>. Can be stored in fields, async methods, and lambdas. Use Span<T> for synchronous processing, Memory<T> when the buffer needs to survive on the heap or cross async boundaries.
ref struct & readonly ref struct: ref struct types are stack-only (cannot be boxed, used as generic type args, stored in heap, or be a field of a class). Used by Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>. `readonly ref struct` ensures all fields are readonly. Enables safe stack-only memory handling.
stackalloc: stackalloc allocates memory on the stack (fast, no GC pressure). Use with Span<T> for safe access. Available in unsafe and safe contexts (via Span). Be mindful of stack space (~1 MB per thread). Best for small temporary buffers.
Unsafe Code & Pointers: C# supports pointer operations in `unsafe` blocks. Enables direct memory access, pointer arithmetic, and fixed memory. Use for interop and performance-critical code. Requires `/unsafe` compiler option. Prefer Span<T> over raw pointers when possible.
Ref Returns & Ref Locals: ref returns allow methods to return references (avoiding copying). ref locals alias existing variables. `ref readonly` returns read-only references. Useful for performance in large struct manipulation and array-like data structures.
Memory Pool & ArrayPool: ArrayPool<T> reuses arrays to reduce allocation and GC pressure. MemoryPool<T> wraps ArrayPool for Memory<T>. Rent and return buffers. Critical in high-throughput server applications (ASP.NET Core, Dataflow). Always return rented buffers.
WeakReference & Conditional Weak Tables: WeakReference<T> (C# 7+) allows referencing an object without preventing GC. `TryGetTarget(out T target)` checks if alive. ConditionalWeakTable<TKey, TValue> attaches data to objects without extending their lifetime, using ephemeron semantics. Common: attaching metadata, caches, dep tables. Unlike dictionary, keys are compared by reference, and entries auto-remove when key is GC'd.

P/Invoke (Platform Invoke): P/Invoke calls native functions from DLLs using DllImport. Specify CharSet, CallingConvention, EntryPoint. Marshal data between managed and unmanaged memory. Use LibraryImport (source-generated) in .NET 7+ for better performance.
COM Interop: COM interop enables calling COM components from .NET (and .NET components from COM). Use COM import attributes, RCW (Runtime Callable Wrapper). .NET 5+ improved COM activation. Common for Office automation, Windows shell extensions, and legacy COM libraries.
Fixed Size Buffers: Fixed-size buffers (fixed keyword) define inline arrays in structs for interop scenarios. Used in unsafe context. The buffer is embedded in the struct layout, matching native memory layouts. Commonly used with P/Invoke and binary protocol parsing.
Marshal Class: System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal provides methods for allocating/freeing unmanaged memory, converting between managed/unmanaged types, structure layout, COM interop, and size computations. Essential for low-level interop scenarios.
WinRT Interop & COM: WinRT (Windows Runtime) interop via C#/WinRT. Consume Windows APIs directly: `Windows.Storage.StorageFile`, `Windows.Graphics.Imaging`. For classic COM interop, use DllImport and COM interfaces with `[ComImport]` and `Guid`. Wrappers via `dynamic` and `IDispatch`. .NET provides built-in wrappers for common APIs. CsWinRT generates projections from .winmd files.

xUnit.net Basics: xUnit is .NET's most popular test framework. Use [Fact] for parameterless tests, [Theory] with [InlineData], [ClassData], or [MemberData] for parameterized tests. Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) is the standard structure. Use IClassFixture for shared context.
NUnit Basics: NUnit uses [Test], [TestCase], [SetUp], [TearDown], [OneTimeSetUp]. Supports assertions with Assert.That (constraint model), categories, retries, parallel execution. Classic assertions (AreEqual) also work but constraint model is preferred.
Moq (Mocking): Moq creates mock objects for interfaces and classes. Setup method behavior, verify invocations, use Callback for side effects. Supports strict vs loose mocking (default: loose). Combine with It.Is<T>() for argument matching.
FluentAssertions: FluentAssertions provides readable, self-documenting assertions. Supports chaining, object graph comparison, collections, strings, timespans, exceptions, and more. Integrates with xUnit, NUnit, MSTest. Produces detailed failure messages.
TDD with C#: Test-Driven Development cycle: Red (write failing test), Green (write minimal code to pass), Refactor (improve code while tests pass). Tests drive API design. Use parameterized tests for edge cases. Keep tests fast, isolated, and deterministic.
xUnit & Fluent Assertions: xUnit.net is .NET's most popular test framework. `[Fact]` for parameterless tests, `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]`, `[ClassData]`, `[MemberData]` for parameterized. `ITestOutputHelper` for console output. FluentAssertions provides readable assertions: `result.Should().Be(42)`, `collection.Should().HaveCount(3).And.Contain(x => x > 0)`. Alternatives: Shouldly, NUnit.

NuGet Package Manager: NuGet is the package manager for .NET. `dotnet add package` installs packages. `dotnet restore` resolves dependencies. PackageReference in .csproj stores versions. nuget.config controls sources. Use Central Package Management for multi-project solutions.

# Add packages
dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json
dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer --version 8.0.0

# Restore
dotnet restore

# List packages
dotnet list package

dotnet list package --vulnerable  # Check for vulnerabilities

# Pack and publish
# dotnet pack -o ./nupkg
# dotnet nuget push ./nupkg/*.nupkg --api-key <key> --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json

// .csproj snippet
// <PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.28" />
ASP.NET Core Minimal API: ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs provide a concise way to build HTTP APIs with minimal ceremony. Use top-level statements, route handlers with dependency injection, and middleware. Perfect for microservices and simple endpoints.
Entity Framework Core: EF Core is an object-relational mapper (ORM). Models map to database tables via DbContext. Supports migrations, LINQ queries, change tracking, eager/lazy/explicit loading, and providers for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, etc.
Blazor Basics: Blazor builds interactive web UIs using C# instead of JavaScript. Blazor Server runs logic on the server via SignalR. Blazor WebAssembly runs compiled .NET in the browser. Blazor Hybrid embeds in native apps (MAUI, WPF). Components are .razor files.
Dependency Injection: ASP.NET Core has built-in DI with three lifetimes: Singleton (one instance), Scoped (per request), Transient (new each time). Register services in Program.cs. The framework auto-injects into constructors of controllers, minimal APIs, and middleware.
Configuration & Options: .NET supports configuration from JSON, environment variables, CLI args, and more via IConfiguration. Options pattern with IOptions<T> (reloadable), IOptionsSnapshot<T> (scoped, reloads per request), IOptionsMonitor<T> (singleton, observes changes). Strongly-typed settings with validation.

Source Generators: C# 9+ source generators run at compile-time to emit C# source files. Create an IncrementalGenerator implementing IIncrementalGenerator. Access syntax trees, semantic models, and attributes. Used by System.Text.Json, Regex, and MediatR for compile-time code gen.
Compile-Time Code Generation with Roslyn: Roslyn (the C# compiler platform) provides APIs for syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation, and compilation. Use CSharpSyntaxTree, SemanticModel, Compilation, and SyntaxGenerator to build or analyze code programmatically.
Native AOT Compilation: Native AOT (Ahead-of-Time) compiles .NET directly to native code (no JIT/IL). Enables fast startup, small self-contained binaries, no runtime compilation. Limited to compatible APIs (no reflection by default). Enable with `<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>` in .csproj.

<!-- .csproj -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
    <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
    <StripSymbols>true</StripSymbols>
  </PropertyGroup>

Function Pointers (delegate*): C# 9 function pointers (`delegate*<T>`) enable efficient native-like function pointer calls without delegate allocation. Used in unsafe contexts for interop and high-performance callbacks. More efficient than delegates (no object allocation).
Regex Source Generators: C# 11+ Regex source generators ([GeneratedRegex]) compile regular expressions at build time. Eliminates runtime compilation (!), provides IntelliSense, and is AOT-compatible. RegexOptions regex options can be passed declaratively.
Raw String Literals: C# 11 raw string literals use triple quotes `"""..."""` for multi-line strings. No escaping needed for quotes, backslashes. Indentation is determined by the closing `"""` position. Perfect for JSON, XML, SQL, regex embedded in code.
Interceptors (Experimental): Interceptors (C# 12 experimental) allow a source generator to replace a method call with a different implementation at compile time. Used for advanced AOP scenarios. Requires `[InterceptsLocation]` attribute. Still experimental, could change.
List Patterns: C# 11 list patterns enable matching on arrays and lists in switch expressions. Supports slice patterns (`..`), discard (`_`), nested patterns. Useful for parsing, validation, and sequence matching without manual indexing.

Collection Expressions: Collection expressions (C# 12) simplify collection creation: `int[] a = [1, 2, 3];`, `List<int> list = [1, 2, 3];`, `Span<int> span = [1, 2, 3];`. Spread operator `..` merges collections: `int[] both = [..first, ..second];`. Works with arrays, spans, `List<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`, and custom collection types via `[CollectionBuilder]`. Supports `ReadOnlySpan<T>` for zero-allocation.
Default Lambda Parameters: C# 12 allows default parameter values in lambdas. Works with both lambda expressions and method group conversions. The default applies when the argument is omitted at the call site.
ref readonly Parameters: C# 12 `ref readonly` parameters combine ref (pass by reference, avoid copy) with readonly (guarantee caller's value is not modified). Best for large readonly structs. The caller provides data without defensive copies.
Alias Any Type: C# 12 global/using aliases can refer to any type, not just named types. Tuple types, array types, pointer types, nullable types — all can be aliased. Improves readability for complex type signatures.
params Collections: C# 12 extends `params` to work with `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and `IEnumerable<T>` beyond just arrays. The compiler creates the collection efficiently with no allocation when using span overloads.
Primary Constructors: Primary constructors (C# 12) for non-record classes/structs. Parameters are in scope for all members. Can initialize fields, properties. Useful for DI, simple initialization, reducing boilerplate. Parameters become captured by the class — compile to fields when accessed. Combine with `readonly` modifier. Record primary constructors existed since C# 9.

Small Methods (Fits in Your Head): Mark Seemann's core heuristic: methods should fit in your head — at most ~10–15 lines. Small methods reduce cognitive load, simplify testing, and force good naming. Extract until you can't extract anymore; each method does one thing at one level of abstraction.
Command-Query Separation: CQS (from Bertrand Meyer, popularized by Seemann) says: a method should be a command (mutates state, returns void/Task) OR a query (returns a value, no side effects), never both. This makes code predictable, testable, and safe to compose.
Pure Functions & Determinism: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects (no I/O, no mutation). Pure functions are trivial to test, cache, parallelize, and reason about. Push side effects to the edges of your architecture.
Cyclomatic Complexity & Guard Clauses: Cyclomatic complexity measures independent paths through code. Keep each method's complexity ≤ 4 (1 + number of decisions). Use guard clauses (early return) to flatten nesting. Extract conditional logic into well-named methods.
API Surface & Information Hiding: Minimize the public API surface of each type. Mark everything `private` by default, then promote only what external consumers need. Fewer public members = less coupling, easier refactoring, simpler testing. Apply the Interface Segregation Principle.
Property-Based Testing: Property-Based Testing (from FsCheck for .NET) tests general properties/ invariants instead of specific examples. The framework generates random inputs to find edge cases. Properties like: roundtrip, idempotence, commutativity, and invariant preservation.
SUT & Test Data Builders: Test Data Builder pattern (from Growing Object-Oriented Software) constructs test objects with sensible defaults and explicit overrides. Avoids repetitive Arrange code, makes tests readable, and isolates test changes when constructors change.
Postel's Law & Defensive Coding: Postel's Law: "Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept." Accept flexible inputs (handle edge cases gracefully) but produce strict, predictable outputs. Use null checks, validation, and normalization at boundaries.
Dependency Inversion & Composition Root: Depend on abstractions, not concretions. Build a Composition Root (the entry point of the application) where all dependencies are wired together. This enables unit testing with mocks, delayed decisions about implementations, and parallel development.
Parameter Objects & Immutability: Replace long parameter lists (3+ parameters) with a parameter object. Using `record` types gives you immutability, value equality, and deconstruction for free. Parameter objects make call sites self-documenting and simplify method evolution.
